title: 1950 profile: marrying Evelyn, radio and his fishing boat
summary: The article says he met Evelyn in 1924 and married rather than studying at the Boston Conservatory, then settled into radio orchestras.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives

blocks.x: all of a sudden." Morehouse met his wife, Evelyn, in 1924 when he was supposed to be preparing to enter the Boston Conservatory of Music, his father's idea. "I was supposed to enter in September," Morehouse said. "I had my choice, marry Evelyn and play jazz music or put it off, study theory and harmony. And we got married in August. That settled it."

The Morehouses have two children, James 19 and Suzanne 15. "When Jimmy came along, I knew I'd have to settle down," Morehouse said. "I'd been in radio since 1928 and I hadn't made up my mind to stay. That clinched it." He's been in radio orchestras ever since. At present he plays in the studio orchestras of the NBC programs, the City Service Band, Break the Bank and the Sunday Longine Hour. In his spare time, Morehouse goes fishing on Great South Bay. He's the proud owner of a 25 foot cruiser, the Sueve II, part of the fleet of the South Shore Power Squadron. "The greatest contribution to American music in the 20th century," Morehouse says, "is Dixieland jazz." "And don't believe it's old hat or losing popularity," he said. "The proof of that is in the youngsters have a record collection that will go through the floor if they get any more. They think it's something new and fascinating. And jazz started something like 50 years ago."
